video.title: IT'S NOT OVER UNTIL YOU WIN - Georgia Dome (Les Brown's Greatest Hits)

motivational.video_read: This is Les Brown's full classic 'It's not over until you win' convention speech: thirty minutes of personal-humiliation stories (labelled educable mentally retarded, sleeping in his office, people laughing at him) converted into vows and call-and-response affirmations. The material lives everywhere in it — the Connect Four story, the Mr. Washington thread, the Penobscot Building story — and it is the densest stretch of publishable moments I have read in this category.

near_misses.why_not: The reframe that dreams are given to us for the purpose of accomplishing them is genuinely interesting, but the sentence arrives convoluted and depends on the 'think about your dream' framing before it; unsure it completes for a cold stranger.
The shoeshine creativity anecdote is charming but the takeaway is sales craft — amaze your customers — aimed at the convention audience; nothing shifts in how the 2am viewer sees themselves.
A call-and-response recap of affirmations; it summarises the speech rather than delivering a landing of its own.
Goal-writing and planning walkthrough — correct and administrative, no charge, changes nothing about who the viewer is.

The 'if you know the why, you can endure almost any how' line is quotable but arrives garbled ('less nietzsche said') and folded into the mother-home anecdote, so it does not cut out cleanly on its own.

skipped.what: opening address and 'think about your dream' framing
dream, risk-takers and biography of humble beginnings — setup, not a landing
fear of failure/comfort/worthiness list plus his résumé of achievements (book, specials, talk show)
customer-service and integrity advice aimed at the distributor audience
continuation of the hard-times story past the envelope payoff
'you're the one' repetition and tape-listening setup
buying his mother a home and the birth-mother adoption story — moving, but it lands as emotion without a turn for the viewer until L0234
closing recaps, handshakes and the hungry chant

clips.title: It's not over until I win
clips.why: The most-marked moment in the video by a mile (69 likes on one comment, 25 more viewers marked it). A father beats his nine-year-old ten straight games and quits; the kid plays to game eleven, wins, yawns and says the exact words the father said. The mirror is the detonation — the viewer hears a child hand them the attitude they are missing. Every line earns its place in the build.

clips.why: The application that follows the story, and the single most-quoted passage in the video — the comment giving the timestamp has 952 likes. The litany is aimed at the exact 2am viewer: a rejection, a no, somebody who said you can count on me and didn't, the car repossessed, the lights cut off — and still reviewing the dream every day. It converts the story's child-logic into an adult vow.

clips.title: Someone's opinion of you does not have to become your reality
clips.why: A boy who has been told he is mentally deficient is told by a teacher, 'don't ever say that again.' This names the private label almost every viewer carries from school or family and hands them the sentence that takes it off — one of the most quoted lines Brown ever said, and the pause before 'reality' is where it lands.

clips.title: I'm the one
clips.why: The emotional peak of the speech. A boy who failed history and English, feeling like a failure, sneaks into a graduation speech, chases the teacher into the parking lot — 'I got these big dreams... I dream of buying my mama home, could I do that, Mr. Washington?' — 'It's possible, Mr. Brown' — and then, broken by the pauses, 'I'm the one... I'm the... one.' The viewer who has never once claimed their own dream feels this in the chest. Long, but every second is the build; the second pass can trim the auditorium speech if needed.

clips.title: It's hard changing your life
clips.why: The humiliation named without self-pity: an entrepreneur sleeping in his office, handed an envelope from management — 'this is an office tower, it's not a hotel, please do not sleep in your office' — and answering it with 'things are bad for me but they're not going to be this way always.' Anyone who has been quietly broke and pretending recognises this lobby. The landing line is the viewer's own sentence now.

clips.title: No matter how bad it is or how bad it gets, I'm going to make it
clips.why: The adoptive mother who didn't know how she would raise two babies becomes the bridge to the viewer's own unknowable dream — 'you don't know how you're going to make this happen but you just feel within yourself some way, somehow' — then the call-and-response vow, said slowly, twice. An instruction sized to be repeated tonight, in the viewer's own mouth.

clips.title: Don't stop running towards your dream
clips.why: Addressed directly at the person in hardship: 'it's a long shot from liberty city, an abandoned building, never knowing my mother or father, no college training, labelled educable mentally — but I kept running toward my dreams.' Then the measured silences and the three 'don't stop's. The pauses are the performance; on the page it looks plain, in the ear it is the point of the whole speech.

clips.title: You were so crazy — I know, but I'm rich
clips.why: The payoff of the whole Mr. Washington thread as a standalone joke with a blade in it. The old teacher calls: 'You were the one, weren't you? ... And you were so crazy.' 'I know — but I'm rich.' It is permission to be called crazy by everyone who doubted you, delivered with a laugh. Sarcasm carrying a real truth.

clips.title: That dream you're holding in your mind — it's possible

'I don't care how far-fetched it might appear, I don't care how disappointing it might have been as you've been working toward that dream — but here's what I know: that dream that you're holding in your mind, it's possible.' It reaches the person whose dream has already disappointed them, which is the only person who needs to hear it.
